greeting: Good morning, Bay View, and happy Saturday. It's a cold, clear start, but the sun is out all day with a high in the mid-40s and an even nicer Sunday ahead. Today we've got the fallout from Friday's nationwide flight shutdown at Mitchell, pie for a good cause at Outpost, and a Bay View music landmark in the spotlight.

top.title: Nationwide ground stop strands travelers at Mitchell Airport
top.dek: A four-hour FAA halt on departures Friday scrambled plans at MKE; airlines warn delays may linger this weekend.
top.body:
A rare nationwide ground stop held every departing flight in the U.S. on the ground for more than four hours Friday afternoon and evening, leaving travelers at Milwaukee Mitchell International Airport stuck at gates and rebooking on the fly. The FAA ordered the stop shortly before 3 p.m. Central after a telecommunications problem disrupted communications with regional air traffic control centers, according to CBS 58.

Planes already in the air were allowed to land, but departures were held until the FAA lifted the stop Friday evening. Federal officials said there was no sign of a cyberattack. It was the first nationwide grounding since an FAA computer outage in January 2023.

If you're flying out of Mitchell this weekend, check with your airline before heading to the airport: carriers warned that planes and crews left out of position could mean more delays and cancellations through the weekend. Neighbors in the Bay View Town Hall group noticed the upside, too: an unusually quiet night under the flight path.

image.alt: Travelers inside Milwaukee Mitchell International Airport during Friday's ground stop

top.title: Outpost's Buy a Slice pie fundraiser is today on KK
top.dek: Grab a slice of pie for a suggested $5 donation at Outpost, 11 a.m. to 2 p.m.
top.body:
Outpost Natural Foods is holding its annual Buy a Slice fundraiser today from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. Stop in and get a slice of the co-op's pie for a suggested $5 donation; the co-op's posts feature its apple pie.

The event runs at Outpost's stores, including the Bay View store at 2826 S. Kinnickinnic Ave. It's also a good moment to look at Thanksgiving: Outpost is taking online orders for full holiday meals, sides and desserts, and has been introducing the Wisconsin farms that raise its turkeys.

openings.title: At Random's Magic Forest returns, with hut reservations opening Nov. 25
openings.dek: The Delaware Ave. lounge is turning its patio into a lit-up winter hideaway of heated cocktail huts again.
openings.body:
At Random, the cocktail lounge at 2501 S. Delaware Ave., says its Magic Forest is coming back for the holidays. The patio becomes a winter hideaway of heated cocktail huts and holiday lights, a seasonal tradition at the bar.

Reservations open Nov. 25, and the bar strongly recommends booking. Hut charges are added to your tab; check the post for current pricing. Kids are welcome until 8 p.m., and it's 21 and over after that. An opening date for the huts hasn't been posted yet.

spotlight.title: Spotlight: Cactus Club
spotlight.dek: From a 1950s country bar to the room where the White Stripes played: Bay View's tiny, all-ages music landmark.
spotlight.body:
Cactus Club is a small music venue and bar on a residential corner at S. Wentworth and E. Russell avenues. Its stage room holds about 200 people and books bands almost every night, most of them all ages, while the front bar keeps its own calendar of DJ happy hours, karaoke and club meetups.

The building is much older than the club. OnMilwaukee's Urban Spelunking series traced a tavern there to at least 1907, and found that police raided an Italian anarchist circle that met inside in 1917. Cliff and Alice Rose turned it into a country-western bar called the Cactus Club in the late 1950s (the club's own history says 1957; OnMilwaukee says 1958), which explains the name. Eric Uecke took over in 1996 and built it into one of the city's essential indie and punk rooms. Kelsey Kaufmann, who started working there in 2011 and ran the booking from 2016, bought the club in February 2020, just weeks before the pandemic shut music venues down.

The roster of bands that played the room on the way up is long. The club lists the White Stripes, Queens of the Stone Age, Death Cab for Cutie, Interpol, Bright Eyes and Low, and Milwaukee Record has reported that the White Stripes played their first out-of-state show there in 1999. In January 2020 it became the first Milwaukee venue to use a new all-ages license, a rule change it had pushed for with Girls Rock Camp.

Under Kaufmann the club has also become a community space through Cactus+, an arts nonprofit started in 2022: open decks where anyone can DJ, a knitting club, queer karaoke, a book club, workshops and markets. It rebuilt its front entrance for wheelchair access, too. Jack White played a surprise fundraiser there in October 2024 and, according to Milwaukee Record and WPR, gave $20,000 in 2025 to cover a city-required curb bump-out. The finished ramp includes a mosaic by artist Kate Klingbeil.

This weekend brings a free Open Decks session today at 1 p.m., two bills tonight, and Sunday's free Milwaukee Record Halftime Show at 11:30 a.m. Squirrel Flower and Sour Widows play Thursday. The club also just announced that its Cactus Winter Market returns Sunday, Dec. 13, from noon to 4 p.m., with vendors to be revealed.

Cactus Club, 2496 S. Wentworth Ave. Open Monday and Tuesday 6 p.m. to midnight; Wednesday and Thursday 4 p.m. to midnight; Friday 4 p.m. to 2:30 a.m.; Saturday 1 p.m. to 2:30 a.m.; Sunday 11 a.m. to 10 p.m. cactusclubmilwaukee.com, @cactusclubmke on Instagram.

buzz.headline: Is Christmas on KK coming back? An organizer says yes
buzz.body: A neighbor asked whether Christmas on KK is happening this year, and a commenter who says he's organizing it answered that it's back and they're just getting organized, sharing a vendor application. One vendor chimed in that she'll be set up at the Magnet Factory on Dec. 11 from 5 to 9 p.m. We haven't seen an official announcement or full schedule yet, so treat the date as tentative.

buzz.headline: Every car on Logan Avenue woke up to a ticket, neighbors say
buzz.body: A neighbor posted Friday morning that every car parked on his stretch of Logan Avenue had a parking ticket, with no obvious reason why. The post drew nearly 100 comments, ranging from theories about revenue to people swapping stories of similar block-wide ticketing. No explanation from the city had surfaced by Saturday morning.

buzz.headline: Lost Whale roasts Holey Mackerel, then signs up anyway
buzz.body: Lost Whale took a playful jab at its "best enemies" at Holey Mackerel, saying they're "actually doing something cool for once": a Merry Mackerel Holiday Village in Greenfield. Lost Whale says it's on board and is pitching local businesses on sponsorships due by Nov. 15. The fine print gives the feud away: the sponsor contact on the flyer has a Lost Whale email address.

buzz.headline: The ground stop gave Bay View a rare quiet night
buzz.body: With every departure in the country grounded Friday, neighbors under the Mitchell flight path noticed the silence, and one joked that at least everyone would get a quiet night's sleep. Another asked whether there were ways to help stranded travelers, thinking of how Canadians took in stuck flyers in 2001. Flights resumed Friday evening; see our top story for travel tips.

history.title: Groppi's: the 1913 Italian grocery that got a second life
history.text: In November 2003, months after the last Groppi closed it, the 90-year-old Italian grocery at Russell and Wentworth reopened under new owners. It's still there.
history.body:
For generations, the corner of E. Russell and S. Wentworth avenues meant one thing to Bay View's Italian families: Groppi's. The Groppi family, Italian immigrants, opened their grocery there in 1913, and their twelve children all worked in the store, according to the Wisconsin Historical Society's property record.

The building is older than the store. The historical society says it began around 1900 as a double workers' cottage built by the Milwaukee Iron Co., the rolling mill company Bay View grew up around, and the cottage can still be seen at the back. A brick storefront went on in 1923 and an addition in 1924. It counts as a contributing building in the Bay View Historic District, listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1982, and the society describes it as the only Italian grocery on Milwaukee's south side.

In February 2003, Tom Groppi, the last of the Groppi children to run it, closed the store. That November it reopened under John Nehring and Anne Finch-Nehring, who owned other Milwaukee-area groceries. They kept the Groppi name and added a deli, a fresh meat counter and a small bar in the back, according to Spectrum News and Urban Milwaukee.

The store changed hands again in January 2024, when brothers Ryan and Casey Foltz took over, leasing the building and keeping the G. Groppi name with Tom Groppi's blessing, Urban Milwaukee reported. Casey Foltz also owns Puddler's Hall down the street, which serves the market's paninis.
